# Running it {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Two lines

```python
mf.write_input()
success, buff = mf.run_model(silent=True, report=True)
```

::: {.fragment}
`write_input()` turns the FloPy objects into a dozen text files.
`run_model()` shells out to the compiled binary and captures its output.
:::

## The three details

::: {.incremental}
1. **FloPy does not raise when a model fails.** It returns
   `(success, buff)` and carries on
2. **`report=True` is not optional** — with `silent=True` alone, `buff` comes
   back **empty**
3. `silent=True` only suppresses the console echo; the full log always goes to
   the `.list` file
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
```python
assert success, "MODFLOW did not converge:\n" + "\n".join(buff[-20:])
```
Every run. Every time. Without `report=True` that message is blank.
:::

## Your turn: spot what's missing

This code runs a model and reports success — and it has a bug that will cost
somebody a day.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_bug
options = {
    "a": "run_model is missing report=True, so buff will be empty",
    "b": "write_input should come after run_model",
    "c": "silent=True suppresses the .list file",
    "d": "there is no bug",
}
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_bug
# mf.write_input()
# success, buff = mf.run_model(silent=True)
# assert success, "did not converge:\n" + "\n".join(buff[-20:])

answer = ______
print(options[answer])
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_bug"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The assertion is correct in shape. Think about what will actually be *in* the
message when it fires.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_bug"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
answer = "a"
```

The code is right in every visible way and the failure message will be empty.
That is the worst kind of bug: it only shows up when something else has already
gone wrong, at which point you have no diagnostic and no idea why.

`silent=True` does **not** suppress the `.list` file — that is always written, and
it is where the real diagnosis lives.
:::
:::

# Test what you can predict {background-color="#AB0520"}

## The most important habit in the module

Before you trust a model on a problem you cannot solve by hand, **run it on one
you can.**

::: {.fragment}
One layer, two constant heads, no stresses. The solution is a straight line.
:::

## Why that matters

::: {.incremental}
- Now, when a later result surprises you, the surprise is about the **physics you
  added**
- Not about whether you set the model up correctly
- Which are very different debugging problems
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
This is the same argument as Week 9's: validate against something you already
know before you trust the thing you don't.
:::

## But check the arithmetic too

Darcy's law over the 2,000 m domain says **5,000 m³/d**. MODFLOW's budget says
**5,263 m³/d**.

::: {.fragment}
A 5% gap. Small enough to look like rounding, large enough to matter.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**A constant head is specified at the cell *centre*, not at the model edge.** The
flow path is 19 cells, not 20 — 1,900 m, not 2,000.
:::

::: {.fragment}
$10 \times \dfrac{10}{1900} \times 100{,}000 = 5263$ m³/d. Exact.
:::

## Your turn: the half-cell

Same idea on a different grid: 250 m cells, 60 columns, heads of 700 m and 620 m
at the two boundary columns.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_halfcell
ncol = 60
delr = 250.0
east_head, west_head = 700.0, 620.0
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_halfcell
naive_distance = ______
true_distance = ______
print(f"naive gradient {(east_head - west_head) / naive_distance:.6f}")
print(f"true gradient  {(east_head - west_head) / true_distance:.6f}")
print(f"error          {100 * (naive_distance / true_distance - 1):.2f} %")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_halfcell"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The naive distance is the full domain width. The true one is centre-to-centre —
one cell shorter.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_halfcell"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
naive_distance = ncol * delr
true_distance = (ncol - 1) * delr
```

15,000 m versus 14,750 m — a 1.7% error. Smaller than the 10-column case, because
the half-cell at each end is a smaller share of a longer domain.

**The practical rule: a boundary condition sits half a cell inside the edge you
drew.** On a 250 m grid that is 125 m of slop, and it is the first thing to check
when a modelled gradient won't match an observed one.
:::
:::

# The `.list` file {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Where a failure explains itself

```
FAILED TO MEET SOLVER CONVERGENCE CRITERIA            1  TIME(S)
BUDGET PERCENT DISCREPANCY IS -162.7401
STOPPING SIMULATION
```

::: {.fragment}
Two separate facts. The solver gave up, **and** water is not being conserved by a
factor of more than two.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The second number is the one to look at first. A converged model with a 5%
discrepancy is also broken — it just didn't say so.
:::

## Reading the budget

```
           IN:                          OUT:
     STORAGE =      0.0000        STORAGE =      0.0000
CONSTANT HEAD =   5263.1582  CONSTANT HEAD =   5263.1582
    TOTAL IN =   5263.1582      TOTAL OUT =   5263.1582
    IN - OUT =      0.0000
PERCENT DISCREPANCY =   0.00
```

::: {.fragment}
Every term, in and out, and the discrepancy at the bottom. **Read this every
time** — it is the only place the model tells you where the water went.
:::

## Your turn: is this budget acceptable?

Four models converged. Which of their budgets would you report?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_budget
runs = {
    "A": 0.00,
    "B": -0.04,
    "C": 3.10,
    "D": -162.74,
}
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_budget
acceptable = [name for name, pct in runs.items() if ______]
print(f"acceptable: {acceptable}")
print(f"rejected:   {[n for n in runs if n not in acceptable]}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_budget"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

The convention is well under 1% in absolute value. `abs()` matters — the sign
tells you which way it is off, not whether it is acceptable.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_budget"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
acceptable = [name for name, pct in runs.items() if abs(pct) < 1.0]
```

`A` and `B`. `C` at 3.1% has converged and is still losing water somewhere —
usually a boundary condition doing something you did not intend. `D` did not
converge at all.

**A converged model with a 3% discrepancy is not a slightly worse answer than one
at 0.04% — it is an answer with an unexplained flux in it**, and until you find
that flux you do not know which of your budget terms is wrong.
:::
:::

## Two formats for the same number

```
 PERCENT DISCREPANCY =   -162.74   PERCENT DISCREPANCY =   -162.74
 BUDGET PERCENT DISCREPANCY IS -162.7401
```

::: {.fragment}
One uses `=` and repeats itself in two columns; the other uses `IS`.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Splitting on `"="` works on the first and crashes on the second. **Take the last
whitespace-separated token** and both work — the kind of thing real file formats
always do to you.
:::

## Wrap up {.smaller}

::: {.kicker}
The three checks, on every run
:::

1. **`success`** — with `report=True`, or the message is empty
2. **Percent discrepancy** — near zero, or the answer is not conserving mass
3. **A case you can predict** — before trusting one you can't
